paras: The whipping of Bill Criswell was a mob assault in August 1895 in which residents of Guthrie, Missouri, caught Criswell, a Black man, and beat him with buggy whips. According to the only report found, he had paraded the village streets with a gun to protest how his friend Emmett Divers had been "disposed of". The Mexico Weekly Ledger reported the beating as a deserved lesson.

Criswell lived near Guthrie, which the Ledger, published at Mexico, placed in "this county", and he had formerly lived in Mexico. The paper described him as a friend of Emmett Divers and said he "became offended at the manner in which" Divers "was disposed of".

In the Ledger's account, Criswell took a gun, paraded the streets of the village, "abused the mob" and was "generally obstreperous". The paper said the citizens of the town "became wearied of this sort of behavior", caught him and gave him "a sound thrash ing with buggy whips". Three whips were worn out on him before a halt was called; the item names none of the men involved and gives no date.
No report of an arrest, complaint or official response appears in the coverage.

The story appeared once, as a short front-page item headed "Negro Whipped." in the Mexico Weekly Ledger of August 22, 1895. Its tone was mocking: it called Criswell a colored "gemmen", spoke of the "trifing [trifling] negro's carcass", and closed by calling him "a noisy, worthless sort of a darkey". The Ledger presented the whipping as a check on his protest, remarking that the next time he wanted to "parade and assert his rights he won't do it."
No other white paper and no Black paper carrying the story was found, so Criswell's own account and that of his neighbors do not survive in the coverage.

accounts.label: Mexico Weekly Ledger local item
accounts.gist: Criswell, angered at how Divers was disposed of, paraded Guthrie's streets armed and abused the mob; wearied citizens caught him and wore out three buggy whips on him. The account of his conduct comes only from this paper, which sided with the whippers.

framing.detail: Headed 'Negro Whipped.', the item calls Criswell a 'trifling negro' and 'worthless sort of a darkey' and treats the beating as a lesson against asserting 'his rights'.

Main account of the Divers lynching at the Calwood bridge, Callaway County, Thursday morning; uses the phrase 'disposed of then and there'. No mention of Criswell or Guthrie.
